title: Position: Mechanisms for Aggregated Individual Reporting Should be Established for Post-Deployment Evaluation
claim: A reporting mechanism links a deployed system's affected population to evaluations, with downstream accountability depending on who owns the mechanism.
layout: Circular cycle of 5 nodes, clockwise arrows, mechanism region shaded green
description: A cyclic diagram of the framework's components, with curved translucent arrows running clockwise. A bold mustard-yellow rounded box labeled 'Evaluated system' (monitor icon) sits at top left and draws the eye first. An arrow labeled 'induces an' leads to 'Affected population' (group icon, yellow) at top right. A green arrow labeled 'submits reports' leads down to '(Online) aggregation' (network and magnifier icons) inside a pale green rounded region captioned 'Aggregated individual reporting mechanism'. A green arrow labeled 'generates/computes' leads left to 'Evaluation' (checklist icon). From Evaluation, a yellow arrow labeled '1st-party mechanism owner' returns to the evaluated system. A blue arrow labeled '2nd or 3rd party mechanism owner (e.g., government)' leads to a '3rd party' node (building icon). A blue arrow labeled 'has power to hold accountable' returns to the system. Colors encode actors: yellow for the system side, green for the mechanism, blue for the third party.
caption: The components of our framework and how they interact. Any evaluated system will have an associated affected population. Members of this population can submit reports to the AIR, which uses collected reports to compute an evaluation that reflects the aggregated experiences among submissions. Potential downstream actions may depend on who the mechanism administrator is.
abstract: The need for developing model evaluations beyond static benchmarking, especially in the post-deployment phase, is now well-understood. At the same time, concerns about the concentration of power in deployed AI systems have sparked a keen interest in "democratic" or "public" AI. In this work, we bring these two ideas together by proposing mechanisms for aggregated individual reporting (AIR), a framework for post-deployment evaluation that relies on individual reports from the public. An AIR mechanism allows those who interact with a specific, deployed (AI) system to report when they feel that they may have experienced something problematic; these reports are then aggregated over time, with the goal of evaluating the relevant system in a fine-grained manner. This position paper argues that individual experiences should be understood as an integral part of post-deployment evaluation, and that the scope of our proposed aggregated individual reporting mechanism is a practical path to that end. On the one hand, individual reporting can identify substantively novel insights about safety and performance; on the other, aggregation can be uniquely useful for informing action. From a normative perspective, the post-deployment phase completes a missing piece in the conversation about "democratic" AI. As a pathway to implementation, we provide a workflow of concrete design decisions and pointers to areas for future research.
